A video of Srinath Perera giving an interview some time comes to my mind. The topic was the establishment of a DPP independent of AG's department, to which he was opposed. Of course he opposes every measure. He explained that the reason for the delay in many of the files for advice getting delay at the AG's end is that they are overworked and that they have time only to deal with about three or four files a day, if I am can recall correctly. That is the very reason why we should have a separate department to recommend which cases are ready for prosecution and which require more time. If you ask the bar or the AG's department they will oppose the extension just like they oppose the creation of a DPP housed outside the AG's. In England litigants and victims can see the beginning and the end of litigation within a couple of years at the most, in a majority of cases. Lawyers in Sri Lanka are an obstacle to change. Lawyers, especially the senior lawyers, should stop taking cases if they have no time to deal with them without delay. They take every case that comes up and sit on them. One reason for the delay.

The Government's position is founded upon the principle that Parliament, acting in its constituent capacity, possesses the constitutional authority to amend any provision of the Constitution in accordance with Articles 82 and 83, subject to any procedural requirements that the Supreme Court may determine. The Constitution contains no express prohibition rendering the retirement age of judges immutable. Had the framers intended judicial retirement age to be permanently entrenched, they would have expressly excluded it from the scope of constitutional amendment. Its inclusion within the Constitution demonstrates that it remains amenable to amendment through the prescribed constitutional process.

The proposed amendment does not undermine the constitutional principle of judicial independence. Judicial independence is secured principally through guarantees of security of tenure, security of remuneration, decisional independence and protection from arbitrary removal. Those guarantees remain intact notwithstanding an alteration to the constitutionally prescribed retirement age. An amendment extending the retirement age neither authorises the arbitrary removal of judges nor interferes with their adjudicative independence.

Comparative constitutional practice strongly supports the proposition that judicial retirement ages are matters of constitutional policy rather than immutable constitutional principles. The United Kingdom increased the compulsory judicial retirement age from 70 to 75 through the Public Service Pensions and Judicial Offices Act 2022, having previously prescribed retirement under the Judicial Pensions and Retirement Act 1993. Australia constitutionally prescribes judicial retirement at age 70 under section 72 of the Australian Constitution, while Canada fixes retirement at 75 under section 99 of the Constitution Act, 1867. Singapore has similarly amended judicial retirement provisions through constitutional and legislative reform. These examples demonstrate that mature constitutional democracies recognise Parliament's authority to determine the appropriate retirement age in accordance with contemporary public policy and institutional requirements.

The Government may further contend that extending the retirement age pursues legitimate public objectives, including retaining experienced judges, preserving institutional knowledge, responding to increased life expectancy and ensuring continuity within the appellate courts. The assessment of whether such a policy is desirable or effective is a matter for the legislature rather than the judiciary. Courts are concerned with constitutional validity, not the wisdom or merits of legislative policy.

Importantly, the amendment applies generally and uniformly to all judges within the relevant class. It neither appoints nor removes any individual judge, nor does it confer selective benefits or discretionary extensions upon particular office holders. It merely amends one constitutional qualification applicable to the office itself, distinguishing it from legislation directed at identifiable individuals.

Nor should allegations of improper political motive be accepted in the absence of cogent evidence. Constitutional adjudication proceeds on the basis of objective legal principles, and legislation enacted by Parliament enjoys a presumption of constitutionality unless the contrary is established. Mere political speculation is insufficient to invalidate an otherwise lawful constitutional amendment.

Finally, the determination of judicial retirement age falls within Parliament's legislative competence. Provided the constitutional amendment procedure is properly followed, questions concerning the appropriate retirement age, judicial manpower planning and the efficient administration of justice are matters of legislative judgment. Courts should not substitute their own policy preferences for those of Parliament unless the amendment demonstrably infringes an entrenched constitutional limitation.

Comparative Authorities
Sri Lankan Constitution, Articles 82 and 83 – Parliament's constituent power to amend the Constitution.
United Kingdom – Judicial Pensions and Retirement Act 1993; Public Service Pensions and Judicial Offices Act 2022.
Australia – Australian Constitution, s.72.
Canada – Constitution Act, 1867, s.99.
United States – Constitution of the United States, Article III (life tenure during good behaviour).
Singapore – Constitutional and legislative reforms governing judicial retirement and tenure.
Conclusion

Accordingly, the Government may properly submit that the proposed amendment represents a lawful exercise of Parliament's constituent authority. Comparative constitutional jurisprudence demonstrates that judicial retirement ages are matters of constitutional design and legislative policy rather than immutable guarantees of judicial independence. Unless it can be shown that the amendment substantially impairs the institutional independence of the judiciary or was enacted for an unconstitutional purpose, it should be upheld as a valid constitutional amendment enacted in accordance with the procedures prescribed by the Constitution.

පසුගිය දින කිහිපය පුරාම අධ්‍යාපන බලධාරීන් සහ විවිධ වෘත්තීය සමිති නායකයින් විසින් සිදු කළ ප්‍රකාශ දෙස බැලීමේදී, පුරවැසියන් ලෙස අප තුළ බරපතළ නීතිමය සහ සදාචාරාත්මක ප්‍රශ්න කිහිපයක් පැනනැඟී ඇත. විශේෂයෙන්ම අධ්‍යාපන අමාත්‍යවරිය අවස්ථා කිහිපයකදීම සඳහන් කළේ විභාගය පැවැත්වීමට පෙර මේ වන විට පවතින නඩු කටයුතු අවසන් කළ යුතු බවයි. එමෙන්ම නීතිපතිවරයා සමඟ සාකච්ඡා කොට එම නඩු කටයුතු නිමා කරන බවට ද ප්‍රකාශ නිකුත් විය.

මෙහිදී බුද්ධිමත් පුරවැසියන් ලෙස අප මතු කළ යුතු ප්‍රශ්නය මෙයයි:

01. නීතිපතිවරයා නඩු තීන්දු දෙන්නා ද?
අධ්‍යාපන අමාත්‍යවරිය පවසන පරිදි නීතිපතිවරයා යනු රජයේ පාර්ශ්වය නියෝජනය කරන නිලධාරියායි. නඩුවක එක් පාර්ශ්වයක් පමණක් වන නීතිපතිවරයා සමඟ "සාකච්ඡා කොට" නඩු අවසන් කරන්නේ කෙසේද? මෙරට නීති පද්ධතියට අනුව නඩුවක නියෝග නිකුත් කිරීමේ, තීන්දු දීමේ සහ නඩුවක් අවසන් කිරීමේ පරම බලය ඇත්තේ ගරු විනිශ්චයකාරවරුන්ට මිස නීතිපතිවරයාට නොවේ.

02. විනිශ්චයකාරවරුන්ගේ භූමිකාව කුමක්ද?
දේශපාලන අධිකාරිය පවසන පරිදි නීතිපතිවරයා සමඟ කතා කොට නඩු අවසන් කළ හැකි නම්, මේ රටේ ස්වාධීන අධිකරණ පද්ධතියක් සහ විනිශ්චයකාරවරුන් සිටීමේ තේරුම කුමක්ද? විධායකය හෝ වෘත්තීය සමිති නායකයින් පවසන පරිදි අධිකරණ තීන්දු මෙහෙයවිය හැකි බවක් මෙයින් ගම්‍ය වන්නේ නැද්ද?

03. නීතියේ ආධිපත්‍යය පිළිබඳ අවදානම
නඩු වල ඉදිරි නියෝග පිළිබඳව දේශපාලනඥයන් කල්තියා අනාවැකි පළ කිරීම හෝ ඒවා "විසඳන" ආකාරය පිළිබඳ පවසන ප්‍රකාශ, රටේ පොදු ජනතාව නීතිය කෙරෙහි තබා ඇති විශ්වාසය පළුදු කරන්නකි. මෙය හුදෙක් ගුරු විභාගය පිළිබඳ ප්‍රශ්නයක් පමණක් නොව, රටේ සමස්ත නීති ක්ෂේත්‍රයේම ගෞරවය පිළිබඳ ප්‍රශ්නයකි.

නීති ක්ෂේත්‍රයේ නියැලෙන්නන්ගේ සහ මහජනතාවගේ අවධානය පිණිසයි!

ආණ්ඩුවේ සහ වගකිවයුත්තන්ගේ මෙම ප්‍රකාශ පිළිබඳව නීතිඥ ප්‍රජාව මෙන්ම සිවිල් පුරවැසියන් ද දැඩි විමසිල්ලෙන් පසුවිය යුතු කාලය එළඹ ඇත.

මෙහිදී බුද්ධිමත් පුරවැසියන් ලෙස අප මතු කළ යුතු ප්‍රශ්නය මෙයයි:

01. නීතිපතිවරයා නඩු තීන්දු දෙන්නා ද?
අධ්‍යාපන අමාත්‍යවරිය පවසන පරිදි නීතිපතිවරයා යනු රජයේ පාර්ශ්වය නියෝජනය කරන නිලධාරියායි. නඩුවක එක් පාර්ශ්වයක් පමණක් වන නීතිපතිවරයා සමඟ "සාකච්ඡා කොට" නඩු අවසන් කරන්නේ කෙසේද? මෙරට නීති පද්ධතියට අනුව නඩුවක නියෝග නිකුත් කිරීමේ, තීන්දු දීමේ සහ නඩුවක් අවසන් කිරීමේ පරම බලය ඇත්තේ ගරු විනිශ්චයකාරවරුන්ට මිස නීතිපතිවරයාට නොවේ.

02. විනිශ්චයකාරවරුන්ගේ භූමිකාව කුමක්ද?
දේශපාලන අධිකාරිය පවසන පරිදි නීතිපතිවරයා සමඟ කතා කොට නඩු අවසන් කළ හැකි නම්, මේ රටේ ස්වාධීන අධිකරණ පද්ධතියක් සහ විනිශ්චයකාරවරුන් සිටීමේ තේරුම කුමක්ද? විධායකය හෝ වෘත්තීය සමිති නායකයින් පවසන පරිදි අධිකරණ තීන්දු මෙහෙයවිය හැකි බවක් මෙයින් ගම්‍ය වන්නේ නැද්ද?

The Government's position is founded upon the principle that Parliament, acting in its constituent capacity, possesses the constitutional authority to amend any provision of the Constitution in accordance with Articles 82 and 83, subject to any procedural requirements that the Supreme Court may determine. The Constitution contains no express prohibition rendering the retirement age of judges immutable. Had the framers intended judicial retirement age to be permanently entrenched, they would have expressly excluded it from the scope of constitutional amendment. Its inclusion within the Constitution demonstrates that it remains amenable to amendment through the prescribed constitutional process.

The proposed amendment does not undermine the constitutional principle of judicial independence. Judicial independence is secured principally through guarantees of security of tenure, security of remuneration, decisional independence and protection from arbitrary removal. Those guarantees remain intact notwithstanding an alteration to the constitutionally prescribed retirement age. An amendment extending the retirement age neither authorises the arbitrary removal of judges nor interferes with their adjudicative independence.

Comparative constitutional practice strongly supports the proposition that judicial retirement ages are matters of constitutional policy rather than immutable constitutional principles. The United Kingdom increased the compulsory judicial retirement age from 70 to 75 through the Public Service Pensions and Judicial Offices Act 2022, having previously prescribed retirement under the Judicial Pensions and Retirement Act 1993. Australia constitutionally prescribes judicial retirement at age 70 under section 72 of the Australian Constitution, while Canada fixes retirement at 75 under section 99 of the Constitution Act, 1867. Singapore has similarly amended judicial retirement provisions through constitutional and legislative reform. These examples demonstrate that mature constitutional democracies recognise Parliament's authority to determine the appropriate retirement age in accordance with contemporary public policy and institutional requirements.

The Government may further contend that extending the retirement age pursues legitimate public objectives, including retaining experienced judges, preserving institutional knowledge, responding to increased life expectancy and ensuring continuity within the appellate courts. The assessment of whether such a policy is desirable or effective is a matter for the legislature rather than the judiciary. Courts are concerned with constitutional validity, not the wisdom or merits of legislative policy.

Importantly, the amendment applies generally and uniformly to all judges within the relevant class. It neither appoints nor removes any individual judge, nor does it confer selective benefits or discretionary extensions upon particular office holders. It merely amends one constitutional qualification applicable to the office itself, distinguishing it from legislation directed at identifiable individuals.

Nor should allegations of improper political motive be accepted in the absence of cogent evidence. Constitutional adjudication proceeds on the basis of objective legal principles, and legislation enacted by Parliament enjoys a presumption of constitutionality unless the contrary is established. Mere political speculation is insufficient to invalidate an otherwise lawful constitutional amendment.

Finally, the determination of judicial retirement age falls within Parliament's legislative competence. Provided the constitutional amendment procedure is properly followed, questions concerning the appropriate retirement age, judicial manpower planning and the efficient administration of justice are matters of legislative judgment. Courts should not substitute their own policy preferences for those of Parliament unless the amendment demonstrably infringes an entrenched constitutional limitation.

Comparative Authorities
Sri Lankan Constitution, Articles 82 and 83 – Parliament's constituent power to amend the Constitution.
United Kingdom – Judicial Pensions and Retirement Act 1993; Public Service Pensions and Judicial Offices Act 2022.
Australia – Australian Constitution, s.72.
Canada – Constitution Act, 1867, s.99.
United States – Constitution of the United States, Article III (life tenure during good behaviour).
Singapore – Constitutional and legislative reforms governing judicial retirement and tenure.
Conclusion

Accordingly, the Government may properly submit that the proposed amendment represents a lawful exercise of Parliament's constituent authority. Comparative constitutional jurisprudence demonstrates that judicial retirement ages are matters of constitutional design and legislative policy rather than immutable guarantees of judicial independence. Unless it can be shown that the amendment substantially impairs the institutional independence of the judiciary or was enacted for an unconstitutional purpose, it should be upheld as a valid constitutional amendment enacted in accordance with the procedures prescribed by the Constitution.
